Importance-Reweighted Fock-Space Variational Monte Carlo

Zheng Che
Abstract

Fock-space variational Monte Carlo (FS-VMC) evaluates variational quantities by stochastic sampling over discrete many-body configurations. For ab initio electronic Hamiltonians, Born distributions can differ markedly between systems, and a Markov chain that mixes well need not yield low-variance estimators. We introduce importance-reweighted FS-VMC (IR-FS-VMC), which leaves the variational objective unchanged while redesigning its Monte Carlo evaluation. An auxiliary distribution and Hamiltonian-guided proposal define the Markov chain, while an evaluation Markov kernel defines an analytically tractable evaluation distribution. Self-normalized importance reweighting then recovers the Born-distribution expectations entering the energy, gradient, and stochastic reconfiguration (SR) matrix. Controlled comparisons on equilibrium H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} separate Markov-chain acceptance from local-energy fluctuations and optimization behavior. Using one production protocol, calculations for H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} dissociation, 36-site hydrogen lattices, and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} and Fe4​S4\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}} active spaces yield accurate variational energies across different Born distributions and electronic-correlation regimes. Together, these results show that the production protocol can support robust FS-VMC optimization across the electronic-structure regimes studied here.

1 Introduction

Accurate low-energy solutions of interacting electronic Hamiltonians remain a central problem in quantum chemistry and quantum many-body physics. In a finite orbital basis and fixed symmetry sector, the many-body state is represented in a Fock space whose dimension grows combinatorially with system size. Full configuration interaction is exact within this space but scales exponentially, motivating complementary approximations such as coupled-cluster theory,2 selected configuration interaction,14; 45 and matrix-product-state density matrix renormalization group (DMRG).4; 5; 33

Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) provides a complementary route by optimizing an explicit parametrized wave function from stochastic estimates of the Rayleigh quotient and its derivatives.11 In a discrete many-body basis, Fock-space VMC (FS-VMC) evaluates these quantities from sampled configurations and sparse Hamiltonian connections. Related formulations have long been used for lattice Hamiltonians,50; 42; 32; 25; 10; 46 and have also been developed for molecular electronic structure.24; 48; 31; 29 Neural quantum states have substantially enlarged the available variational families,3; 9; 1; 53; 21; 18; 30; 20; 49; 16 while stochastic reconfiguration and related natural-gradient methods have enabled the optimization of increasingly flexible parametrizations.38; 8; 27 Selected-configuration approaches provide complementary alternatives to stochastic evaluation for Fock-space neural states.15; 7; 36

The stochastic procedure remains a separate practical challenge. For molecular electronic Hamiltonians, the Born distribution can become strongly concentrated on a small part of configuration space, making local Markov chains slow to move between probability regions.22; 19; 23; 36 Changing the Markov-chain stationary distribution can improve mixing, but it also changes the importance weights and the fluctuations of the local quantities entering the energy, gradient, and SR matrix. Conversely, a chain with a reasonable acceptance rate need not provide a low-variance estimator. Markov-chain mixing and estimator variance are therefore distinct aspects of the stochastic calculation, and improving one does not in general optimize the other.

Importance sampling provides the formal freedom to evaluate a fixed Born-distribution expectation using another distribution.44; 43; 23 The Markov dynamics can be modified independently through the proposal mechanism,6 and Hamiltonian-guided proposals are well established for sampling connected configurations in Fock space.13 More recently, related work has shown that a post-sampling Markov kernel can regularize local estimators in the presence of wave-function zeros and discrete support mismatch.47 These developments suggest a simple organizing principle: the variational objective is fixed by the Hamiltonian and wave function, whereas its Monte Carlo evaluation need not be tied to direct Born sampling.

Here we develop importance-reweighted Fock-space variational Monte Carlo (IR-FS-VMC) from this separation. A Markov chain samples an auxiliary distribution using a Hamiltonian-guided proposal, and an evaluation Markov kernel generates configurations from an analytically tractable evaluation distribution. Self-normalized importance reweighting then recovers the Born-distribution expectations entering the energy, gradient, and SR matrix, leaving the variational objective and wave-function parametrization unchanged. Using a fixed spin-projected neural backflow ansatz and the same SR optimizer, we first compare Born, tempered, and IR variants for equilibrium H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} to distinguish Markov-chain acceptance, local-energy fluctuations, and optimization behavior. We then apply one production protocol, without system-specific sampling parameters, to H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} bond breaking, 36-site hydrogen lattices, and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} and Fe4​S4\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}} active spaces. These calculations test whether the production protocol can remain stable across electronic-structure problems with different Born distributions and electronic-correlation regimes.

2 Theory

The stochastic evaluation of FS-VMC involves two complementary aspects: generating configurations with efficient Markov-chain dynamics and obtaining low-variance estimators for Born-distribution expectations. In the following, we introduce the importance-reweighting framework that separates these roles by modifying the sampling procedure while preserving the underlying variational objective.

2.1 Fock-Space Variational Monte Carlo

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a finite configuration space in a fixed Fock-space sector, with orthonormal basis states {|x⟩:x∈𝒳}\{\ket{x}:x\in\mathcal{X}\}. For a real parametrized wave function

|ψ𝜽⟩=∑x∈𝒳ψ𝜽​(x)​|x⟩,\ket{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)\ket{x}, (1)

the variational energy is

E⁡(𝜽)=⟨ψ𝜽|H^|ψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩.E(\bm{\theta})=\frac{\braket{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}|\hat{H}|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}{\braket{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}. (2)

Define the Born distribution

p𝜽​(x)=|ψ𝜽​(x)|2Z𝜽,Z𝜽=∑x|ψ𝜽​(x)|2,p_{\bm{\theta}}(x)=\frac{|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|^{2}}{Z_{\bm{\theta}}},\qquad Z_{\bm{\theta}}=\sum_{x}|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|^{2}, (3)

and, where ψ𝜽​(x)≠0\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)\neq 0, the local energy

EL​(x)=⟨x|H^|ψ𝜽⟩ψ𝜽​(x)=∑yHx​y​ψ𝜽​(y)ψ𝜽​(x),E_{\mathrm{L}}(x)=\frac{\braket{x|\hat{H}|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)}=\sum_{y}H_{xy}\frac{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(y)}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)}, (4)

with Hx​y=⟨x|H^|y⟩H_{xy}=\braket{x|\hat{H}|y}. The energy is then E=𝔼p𝜽​[EL]E=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}}}[E_{\mathrm{L}}].

For the logarithmic derivatives

Oi​(x)=∂θilog⁡|ψ𝜽​(x)|,O_{i}(x)=\partial_{\theta_{i}}\log|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|, (5)

the energy gradient and SR matrix are

gi\displaystyle g_{i} =2​𝔼p𝜽​[Δ​Oi​Δ​EL],\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}}}[\Delta O_{i}\,\Delta E_{\mathrm{L}}], (6)
Si​j\displaystyle S_{ij} =𝔼p𝜽​[Δ​Oi​Δ​Oj],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}}}[\Delta O_{i}\,\Delta O_{j}], (7)

where Δ​A=A−𝔼p𝜽​[A]\Delta A=A-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}}}[A]. The matrix SS is the real part of the quantum geometric tensor and is the matrix used in SR.38; 39 These are Born-distribution expectations; their Monte Carlo evaluation can use a different distribution without changing the variational objective.

2.2 Importance Reweighting

Let r𝜽​(x)=r~𝜽​(x)/Zrr_{\bm{\theta}}(x)=\widetilde{r}_{\bm{\theta}}(x)/Z_{r} be an evaluation distribution satisfying supp⁡(p𝜽)⊆supp⁡(r𝜽)\operatorname{supp}(p_{\bm{\theta}})\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(r_{\bm{\theta}}). Define the unnormalized importance weight

ω𝜽​(x)=|ψ𝜽​(x)|2r~𝜽​(x).\omega_{\bm{\theta}}(x)=\frac{|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|^{2}}{\widetilde{r}_{\bm{\theta}}(x)}. (8)

For any integrable quantity ff,

𝔼p𝜽​[f]=𝔼r𝜽​[ω𝜽​f]𝔼r𝜽​[ω𝜽],\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}}}[f]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{r_{\bm{\theta}}}[\omega_{\bm{\theta}}f]}{\mathbb{E}_{r_{\bm{\theta}}}[\omega_{\bm{\theta}}]}, (9)

so the unknown normalization constants cancel.44; 43

For samples {xn}n=1Ns\{x_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{s}}} from a stationary process with evaluation distribution r𝜽r_{\bm{\theta}}, define

wn=ω𝜽​(xn)∑mω𝜽​(xm),A¯=∑nwn​A​(xn).w_{n}=\frac{\omega_{\bm{\theta}}(x_{n})}{\sum_{m}\omega_{\bm{\theta}}(x_{m})},\qquad\overline{A}=\sum_{n}w_{n}A(x_{n}). (10)

The corresponding self-normalized estimators are

E^\displaystyle\widehat{E} =E¯L,\displaystyle=\overline{E}_{\mathrm{L}}, (11)
g^i\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{i} =2​∑nwn​[Oi​(xn)−O¯i]​[EL​(xn)−E¯L],\displaystyle=2\sum_{n}w_{n}[O_{i}(x_{n})-\overline{O}_{i}][E_{\mathrm{L}}(x_{n})-\overline{E}_{\mathrm{L}}], (12)
S^i​j\displaystyle\widehat{S}_{ij} =∑nwn​[Oi​(xn)−O¯i]​[Oj​(xn)−O¯j].\displaystyle=\sum_{n}w_{n}[O_{i}(x_{n})-\overline{O}_{i}][O_{j}(x_{n})-\overline{O}_{j}]. (13)

They are generally biased at finite sample size because of self-normalization, but are consistent under the usual ergodicity and moment conditions. The same normalized weights apply to other Born-distribution expectations. For correlated samples, Monte Carlo error contains both the fluctuations of the importance-weighted local quantity and its serial correlation along the sampling process. The corresponding long-run variance and support conditions are given in the Supporting Information.

2.3 Sampling and Estimation

For the ab initio calculations, we use the nonrelativistic electronic Hamiltonian in an orthonormal spatial-orbital basis,

H^=Ecore+∑p​q​σhp​q​ap​σ†​aq​σ+12​∑p​q​r​s​σ​τ(p​q|r​s)​ap​σ†​ar​τ†​as​τ​aq​σ.\hat{H}=E_{\mathrm{core}}+\sum_{pq\sigma}h_{pq}a_{p\sigma}^{\dagger}a_{q\sigma}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{pqrs\sigma\tau}(pq|rs)a_{p\sigma}^{\dagger}a_{r\tau}^{\dagger}a_{s\tau}a_{q\sigma}. (14)

Let 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x) denote a symmetric retained set of nonzero off-diagonal Hamiltonian connections, y∈𝒞⁡(x)⇔x∈𝒞⁡(y)y\in\mathcal{C}(x)\Leftrightarrow x\in\mathcal{C}(y), and define the proposal normalization

d⁡(x)=∑y∈𝒞⁡(x)|Hx​y|.d(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{C}(x)}|H_{xy}|. (15)

Define the auxiliary distribution:

ρ𝜽,α​(x)∝d⁡(x)​|ψ𝜽​(x)|α,0≤α≤2.\rho_{\bm{\theta},\alpha}(x)\propto d(x)|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|^{\alpha},\qquad 0\leq\alpha\leq 2. (16)

The exponent α\alpha controls the amplitude concentration of the auxiliary distribution. Reducing α\alpha can facilitate transitions between regions with different wave-function amplitudes, but it also increases the mismatch with the Born distribution and hence the burden on importance reweighting. We therefore treat α\alpha as a finite-system mixing–reweighting tradeoff and adapt it during optimization. The update and the corresponding importance-weight behavior are given in the Supporting Information.

Hamiltonian-connected proposals are drawn from

Q⁡(y|x)=|Hx​y|d⁡(x),y∈𝒞⁡(x),Q(y|x)=\frac{|H_{xy}|}{d(x)},\qquad y\in\mathcal{C}(x), (17)

a form closely related to heat-bath sampling in Fock-space projector Monte Carlo.13 Hermiticity and the symmetric connection set give the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability

a⁡(x,y)=min⁡{1,|ψ𝜽​(y)ψ𝜽​(x)|α},a(x,y)=\min\left\{1,\left|\frac{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(y)}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)}\right|^{\alpha}\right\}, (18)

because the same factor d⁡(x)d(x) appears in the auxiliary distribution and the proposal normalization. The paired choice of ρα\rho_{\alpha} and QQ therefore defines the Markov-chain dynamics.

The configurations entering the estimators are generated from the evaluation Markov kernel

Kβ​(y|x)=(1−β)​δx​y+β​Q​(y|x),0≤β<1.K_{\beta}(y|x)=(1-\beta)\delta_{xy}+\beta Q(y|x),\qquad 0\leq\beta<1. (19)

At fixed α\alpha, KβK_{\beta} does not alter the Markov-chain transition; it changes only the conditional distribution of the evaluation configuration. This redistributes probability mass along Hamiltonian connections and changes the support and fluctuations of the local estimators. Related post-sampling kernels have recently been introduced for support-mismatch problems in discrete VMC.47 Averaging over stationary chain configurations gives the evaluation distribution

r~𝜽,α,β​(y)=(1−β)​d​(y)​|ψ𝜽​(y)|α+β​∑x∈𝒞⁡(y)|Hx​y|​|ψ𝜽​(x)|α.\widetilde{r}_{\bm{\theta},\alpha,\beta}(y)=(1-\beta)d(y)|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(y)|^{\alpha}+\beta\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}(y)}|H_{xy}|\,|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)|^{\alpha}. (20)

The local estimators are evaluated under this evaluation distribution, and the weights in eq. 8 recover the Born-distribution expectations in eqs. 11, 12 and 13. The construction therefore has a direct division of roles: (ρα,Q)(\rho_{\alpha},Q) defines the Markov chain, KβK_{\beta} defines the evaluation distribution, and importance reweighting leaves the variational objective unchanged.

3 Computational Setup

For a two-body ab initio Hamiltonian, exact local-energy evaluation requires wave-function amplitudes on O⁡(Norb4)O(N_{\mathrm{orb}}^{4}) single- and double-excitation connections in the worst case, where NorbN_{\mathrm{orb}} is the number of spatial orbitals. During optimization we therefore partition the off-diagonal Hamiltonian action into deterministic strong connections, |Hx​y|≥ε1|H_{xy}|\geq\varepsilon_{1}, stochastically contracted weak connections, ε2≤|Hx​y|<ε1\varepsilon_{2}\leq|H_{xy}|<\varepsilon_{1}, and an omitted remainder below ε2\varepsilon_{2}. The weak part is estimated from NelocN_{\mathrm{eloc}} stratified samples.28; 34; 48; 31; 49 This semistochastic contraction reduces neural-wave-function evaluations and is independent of the importance-reweighting construction.

The deterministic strong set is also reused as the retained sampler connectivity, 𝒞⁡(x)={y≠x:|Hx​y|≥ε1}\mathcal{C}(x)=\{y\neq x:|H_{xy}|\geq\varepsilon_{1}\}, with integral-based screening.13 Thus ε1\varepsilon_{1} fixes the retained connectivity used by both the local-energy contraction and the sampler, whereas ε2\varepsilon_{2} and NelocN_{\mathrm{eloc}} affect only the local-energy estimator. The Hamiltonian-guided proposal itself requires only the connections of the current chain configuration. For β>0\beta>0, evaluating eq. 20 additionally requires the incoming Hamiltonian contraction; this additional contraction arises from exact marginalization of the Markov kernel, not from the proposal.

All calculations use the same real spin-projected neural backflow ansatz,21; 18 with configuration-dependent spatial orbitals, highest-weight spin projection, and reference-biased initialization. Parameters are optimized by sample-space stochastic reconfiguration37; 38; 8 with a predictor based on the preceding update direction.12 The controlled comparisons use the same wave function, optimizer, sample size, and local-energy settings, changing only the sampling-and-estimation protocol.

The molecular and active-space Hamiltonians are expressed in orthonormal spatial orbitals. Published FCIDUMP Hamiltonians are used for Fe–S active spaces17, while H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and the 36-site hydrogen-lattice integrals are generated with PySCF.40; 41 Independent spin-adapted DMRG reference calculations for the hydrogen lattices are performed with Block2.51; 33 The orbital bases, initial configurations, reference calculations, and all numerical parameters are specified in the Supporting Information.

All calculations were performed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80 GB) with 16 Intel Xeon Platinum 8358 CPU cores and 128 GB of system memory.

4 Results and Discussion

4.1 Sampling and Optimization

We first compare five protocols for equilibrium H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}. Born samples the Born distribution with a symmetric 50:50 single/double proposal. Tempered samples |ψ|α|\psi|^{\alpha} with adaptive α\alpha using the same proposal and reweights all variational quantities to the Born distribution. The three IR protocols use (α,β)=(2,0.5)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,0.5), adaptive α\alpha with β=0\beta=0, and adaptive α\alpha with β=0.5\beta=0.5; the last is the production protocol used elsewhere. The α=2\alpha=2 IR variant removes amplitude tempering while retaining the factor d⁡(x)d(x) in the auxiliary distribution and the Hamiltonian-guided proposal, whereas the β=0\beta=0 variant removes the evaluation displacement by KβK_{\beta}. All other settings are identical.

Equilibrium H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} illustrates a sharp distinction between Markov-chain acceptance and local-energy fluctuations [Fig. 1(a)–(c)]. The Born chain has near-zero acceptance and the optimization stalls. Over iterations 100100–500500, Tempered raises the median acceptance rate to 0.0690.069, but the sampled local-energy variance is 2.51×102​Eh22.51\times 10^{2}\,E_{\mathrm{h}}^{2} and the energy remains far from FCI. Flattening the amplitude dependence of the auxiliary distribution therefore restores transitions without by itself providing a useful optimization estimator. Conversely, IR with α=2\alpha=2 retains a low Markov-chain acceptance rate of 0.00190.0019, yet its local-energy variance is 8.03×10−2​Eh28.03\times 10^{-2}\,E_{\mathrm{h}}^{2} and its median energy error over iterations 901901–10001000 is 5.39​m​Eh5.39\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}}. This shows that low Markov-chain acceptance does not by itself imply large local-energy fluctuations.

For H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}, the complementary β=0\beta=0 run remains close to its initial wave function and the adaptive exponent stays near its initial value on this trajectory. Full IR combines adaptive α\alpha with β=0.5\beta=0.5, reaching a median Markov-chain acceptance rate of 0.0630.063 and a local-energy variance of 3.15×10−2​Eh23.15\times 10^{-2}\,E_{\mathrm{h}}^{2} over iterations 100100–500500, followed by a median error of 1.25​m​Eh1.25\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} over iterations 901901–10001000. Because the adaptive α\alpha update uses evaluation statistics, these ablations are not an additive decomposition of two independent parameters. They nevertheless show that acceptance rate alone does not determine the optimization outcome and that the Markov chain and evaluation distribution address different parts of the stochastic calculation.

Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} provides a contrasting regime [Fig. 1(d)–(f)]. The Born chain already has a median acceptance rate of 0.0780.078 over iterations 100100–500500. The Hamiltonian-guided IR variants increase the Markov-chain acceptance further, while all five protocols reduce the local-energy variance to the 10−3​Eh210^{-3}\,E_{\mathrm{h}}^{2} scale and reach median errors of 0.630.63–1.07​m​Eh1.07\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} over iterations 901901–10001000. Here the standard Born calculation is already viable, so higher acceptance does not translate into a comparably large change in the final energy trajectory. Together, the two systems show why stochastic performance should be assessed from Markov-chain and estimator diagnostics rather than inferred from the electronic-correlation character of the state.

The acceptance rates in Fig. 1 describe the chains used during optimization. To separate this from the final variational accuracy, post-optimization Born-distribution MCMC diagnostics for the optimized H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} series and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} are reported in the Supporting Information.

4.2 Variational Energies

We next assess the common production protocol on systems whose electronic structures span bond breaking, extended hydrogen lattices, and transition-metal active spaces. The comparisons below measure the accuracy of the complete VMC calculation—wave function, optimization, and stochastic procedure—rather than attributing the residual energy error to sampling alone.

For H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}, the IR-FS-VMC error remains 0.1020.102–0.444​m​Eh0.444\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} from equilibrium to 3​Re3R_{\mathrm{e}} [Fig. 2(a)]. At 2​Re2R_{\mathrm{e}} it is 0.263​m​Eh0.263\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}}, compared with 5.5125.512 and 0.943​m​Eh0.943\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} for UCCSDT and MRCISD, respectively.26 Bond stretching changes the occupation structure substantially, as shown below, but no sampling or optimization parameter is retuned along the curve. The sub-millihartree errors therefore establish that the production protocol remains usable from the near-equilibrium closed-shell regime into the stretched, multireference regime. The independent Born-distribution MCMC diagnostics in the Supporting Information vary differently with bond length, further separating Markov-chain behavior from energy error.

The 36-site hydrogen systems extend the comparison to one-, two-, and three-dimensional geometries [Fig. 2(b)]. IR-FS-VMC lies 0.0070.007 and 0.153​m​Eh0.153\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} per atom above the M=1600M=1600 SA-DMRG values for the chain and square lattice and 0.182​m​Eh0.182\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} per atom below the corresponding cubic value. The SA-DMRG energy is essentially converged over the displayed bond dimensions for the chain, whereas it changes by 1.2381.238 and 2.741​m​Eh2.741\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} per atom for the square and cubic lattices between M=100M=100 and 16001600. Accordingly, the cubic M=1600M=1600 point is a finite-bond-dimension variational reference rather than a converged ground-state estimate; an IR-FS-VMC energy below that point is therefore consistent with the variational principle. Across the three geometries, the IR-FS-VMC energies remain within 0.2​m​Eh0.2\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} per atom of the best displayed SA-DMRG values, while the latter show increasingly strong bond-dimension dependence from the chain to the square and cubic lattices.

The Fe–S models probe a different form of many-electron complexity, with dense low-energy spin couplings and substantial multireference character in compact active spaces.35; 17; 52 For Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} (30​e,20​o)(30e,20o), IR-FS-VMC reaches −116.605210​Eh-116.605210\,E_{\mathrm{h}}, 0.399​m​Eh0.399\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} above the M=12000M=12000 SA-DMRG reference. For Fe4​S4\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}} (54​e,36​o)(54e,36o), it reaches −327.240478​Eh-327.240478\,E_{\mathrm{h}}, 4.864​m​Eh4.864\,\mathrm{m}E_{\mathrm{h}} above the extrapolated BS1 SA-DMRG reference.52 The larger residual error for Fe4​S4\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}} should not be assigned to sampling alone; wave-function expressivity and optimization can also contribute at this scale. Taken together with H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and H36\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{36}}}, the energy benchmarks show that IR-FS-VMC can be used without system-specific sampling parameters across markedly different electronic structures.

4.3 Electronic Correlation

Natural occupations and spin correlations provide a compact characterization of the optimized states and establish the physical diversity of the benchmark set independently of the stochastic diagnostics.

The natural occupations span qualitatively different regimes [Fig. 3(a)]. Equilibrium H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} is close to a closed-shell 2/02/0 occupation pattern, whereas bond stretching produces fractional frontier occupations; at 3​Re3R_{\mathrm{e}} four orbitals lie near single occupation. The hydrogen lattices and Fe–S active spaces show broadly fractional spectra. These occupations characterize the multireference structure represented by the optimized wave functions, but they are not used as measures of Markov-chain mixing or estimator variance.

The spin correlations show the corresponding magnetic structure [Fig. 3(b,c)]. The hydrogen lattices exhibit alternating antiferromagnetic correlations over several Manhattan distances. In Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}, the two Fe centers are strongly antiferromagnetically correlated, ⟨𝑺1⋅𝑺2⟩=−5.35\langle\bm{S}_{1}\!\cdot\!\bm{S}_{2}\rangle=-5.35. In Fe4​S4\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}, Fe1–Fe2 and Fe3–Fe4 have positive correlations of about +3.34+3.34, while correlations between the two pairs are about −4.15-4.15, consistent with the BS1 spin-coupling pattern used to initialize the calculation and with the strongly spin-coupled character of these active-space models.35; 52 The contrast with Fig. 1 is deliberate: electronic-correlation diagnostics and stochastic diagnostics describe different aspects of the calculation, and neither is a proxy for the other.

5 Conclusions and Outlook

We have developed IR-FS-VMC, which uses importance reweighting to separate the variational objective from its Monte Carlo evaluation. The energy, gradient, and SR matrix remain Born-distribution expectations, while the Markov-chain dynamics and evaluation distribution can be modified without changing the objective. This formulation separates two statistical questions that are often conflated in practice: Markov-chain mixing and the fluctuations of the resulting importance-weighted estimators.

The controlled H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} and Fe2​S2\text{Fe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} calculations show that Markov-chain acceptance, local-energy fluctuations, and optimization accuracy need not vary together. The broader benchmarks show that the same production protocol yields accurate variational energies for molecular bond breaking, hydrogen lattices, and Fe–S active spaces with substantially different Born distributions and electronic-correlation regimes. Together, these results support the production protocol across the distinct electronic-structure regimes studied here.

The present work addresses sampling and estimation; it does not remove limitations from wave-function expressivity, optimization, or local-energy evaluation. These components can be improved independently and combined with the IR construction, which requires only wave-function amplitudes, sparse Hamiltonian connections, and the Born-distribution observables already used in FS-VMC. It is therefore compatible with other variational ansatzes and optimization schemes. Further tests on larger active spaces and other many-body Hamiltonians will clarify the regime over which a common importance-reweighted protocol remains effective.

he Supporting Information provides estimator properties and support conditions, sampling and optimization details, projected neural backflow and semistochastic local-energy definitions, computational specifications, and post-optimization analysis.
